claim: FMNL2 expressed at the germinal vesicle (GV), metaphase I (MI), and metaphase II (MII) stages during mouse oocyte maturation.
source: The results indicated that FMNL2 all expressed in GV, MI, and MII stages during mouse oocyte maturation (GV, 1; MI, 0.82 ± 0.07; MII, 0.61 ± 0.10, Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by western blotting data showing FMNL2 protein expression levels at different stages (Figure 1A) with quantified relative intensities.

claim: FMNL2 accumulated at the oocyte cortex during the GV, GVBD, MI, and MII stages.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, Fmnl2-EGFP mRNA microinjection showed that FMNL2 accumulated at the oocyte cortex during the GV, GVBD MI, and MII stages.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy images of Fmnl2-EGFP mRNA microinjection and antibody staining (Figure 1B).

claim: FMNL2 localized at the spindle periphery during MI stages.
source: Besides, FMNL2 also localized at the spindle periphery during MI stages.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging showing FMNL2 localization patterns (Figure 1B).

claim: Both FMNL2 and F-actin are localized in the cortex region of oocytes.
source: In addition, we co-stained FMNL2 antibody with F-actin, and the results revealed that both FMNL2 and F-actin are localized in the cortex region of oocytes (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by co-immunofluorescence staining showing colocalization of FMNL2 and F-actin (Figure 1C).

claim: FMNL2 and actin colocalize in porcine oocytes.
source: Similar localization was also found in porcine oocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images of porcine oocytes showing FMNL2 and actin colocalization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Knockdown of FMNL2 significantly decreased FMNL2 protein levels in mouse oocytes.
source: A significant decrease of FMNL2 protein level was shown in FMNL2-KD oocytes compared to control group by western blot (1 vs. 0.48 ± 0.08, p < 0.01, Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis with quantified protein levels showing significant reduction (Figure 2A).

claim: Knockdown of FMNL2 reduced the rate of polar body extrusion in mouse oocytes.
source: The quantitative results also confirmed this phenotype (rate of polar body extrusion: 74.26 ± 1.44%, n = 439 vs. 59.5 ± 2.82%, n = 398, p < 0.001, Figure 2C; rate of large polar bodies: 19.05 ± 1.97%, n = 311 vs. 37.16 ± 1.87%, n = 257, p < 0.0001, Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of polar body extrusion rates with statistical significance (Figure 2C).

claim: Knockdown of FMNL2 increased the rate of large polar body formation in mouse oocytes.
source: The quantitative results also confirmed this phenotype (rate of polar body extrusion: 74.26 ± 1.44%, n = 439 vs. 59.5 ± 2.82%, n = 398, p < 0.001, Figure 2C; rate of large polar bodies: 19.05 ± 1.97%, n = 311 vs. 37.16 ± 1.87%, n = 257, p < 0.0001, Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis showing significantly increased rate of large polar bodies (Figure 2D).

claim: Exogenous Fmnl2 mRNA expression rescued first polar body extrusion defects in FMNL2-depleted oocytes.
source: The quantitative results also confirmed this phenotype (rate of polar body extrusion: 48.34 ± 4.2%, n = 355 vs. 62.62 ± 3.6%, n = 377, p < 0.01, Figure 2H; rate of large polar bodies: 30.93 ± 2%, n = 193 vs. 9.58 ± 2.4%, n = 203, p < 0.01, Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing restored polar body extrusion rates (Figure 2H).

claim: Exogenous Fmnl2 mRNA expression rescued large polar body defects in FMNL2-depleted oocytes.
source: The quantitative results also confirmed this phenotype (rate of polar body extrusion: 48.34 ± 4.2%, n = 355 vs. 62.62 ± 3.6%, n = 377, p < 0.01, Figure 2H; rate of large polar bodies: 30.93 ± 2%, n = 193 vs. 9.58 ± 2.4%, n = 203, p < 0.01, Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing reduced rate of large polar bodies (Figure 2I).

claim: Double knockdown of FMNL2 and FMNL3 did not cause more severe defects in polar body extrusion compared to single knockdown of FMNL2.
source: However, when compared to the single knockdown of Fmnl2, the double knockdown of FMNL2 and FMNL3 did not cause more severe defects in polar body extrusion (polar body extrusion, Control: 70.97 ± 1.23%, n = 261 vs. FMNL2 + 3-KD: 60.42 ± 2.99%, n = 198, p < 0.05, Figure 2J; large polar body, Control: 10.85 ± 0.97%, n = 172 vs. FMNL2 + 3-KD: 32.90 ± 1.88%, n = 118, p < 0.001, Figure 2K).
evidence: Supported by quantitative comparison of single and double knockdown effects (Figure 2J, 2K).

claim: FMNL2 depletion caused spindle migration failure in mouse oocytes.
source: However, in FMNL2-KD oocytes, two phenotypes were observed: (1) the meiotic spindle remained in the center of the oocyte until 10 hr, and then the oocytes initiated the cytokinesis at 10.5 hr but failed to extrude the polar body; (2) some oocytes with arrested spindles initiated the cytokinesis but extruded a big polar body (Figure 3A). This indicated the failure of spindle migration after FMNL2 depletion.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy showing spindles remaining in the center of oocytes (Figure 3A).

claim: The rate of cortex-localized spindles in control oocytes was significantly higher than in FMNL2-KD oocytes.
source: We analyzed the rate of cortex-localized spindle in oocytes by cultured for 9.5 hr, and the result showed that the rate of migrated spindles in control oocytes was significantly higher than that in FMNL2-KD oocytes (59.94 ± 3.42%, n = 78 vs. 38.97 ± 6.34%, n = 64, p < 0.05, Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of spindle migration rates (Figure 3B).

claim: Exogenous Fmnl2 rescued spindle migration defects in FMNL2-depleted oocytes.
source: We also performed FMNL2 rescue experiments. Supplementing with exogenous Fmnl2 rescued the spindle migration defects compared with the FMNL2-depletion group (40.27 ± 3.19%, n = 81 vs. 57.01 ± 2.72%, n = 57, p < 0.01, Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing restored spindle migration rates (Figure 3C).

claim: The L/D ratio of FMNL2-KD oocytes was significantly greater than that of control oocytes at 9.5 hr culture.
source: Our results indicated that by cultured for 9.5 hr, the L/D ratio of the FMNL2-KD oocytes was significantly greater than that of the control oocytes (0.17 ± 0.05, n = 18 vs. 0.24 ± 0.05, n = 18, p < 0.001; Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of spindle positioning using L/D ratio measurements (Figure 3D).

claim: Exogenous FMNL2 rescued the spindle migration defects as measured by L/D ratio in FMNL2-depleted oocytes.
source: Supplementing with exogenous FMNL2 rescued the spindle migration defects compared with the FMNL2-depletion group (0.26 ± 0.04, n = 12 vs. 0.16 ± 0.04, n = 13, p < 0.0001; Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing restored L/D ratios (Figure 3D).

claim: Similar spindle migration defects were observed in porcine oocytes after FMNL2 depletion.
source: Similar results were also observed in porcine oocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data from porcine oocytes showing increased L/D ratio after FMNL2 antibody injection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: There was no significant difference in cortex actin signals between control oocytes and FMNL2-KD oocytes.
source: Surprisingly, there was no significant difference for the signals of cortex actin was observed between control oocytes and FMNL2-KD oocytes, which was confirmed by the fluorescence intensity analysis (30.88 ± 1.10, n = 28 vs. 30.58 ± 1.12, n = 28, p > 0.05, Figure 4A, B).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence intensity analysis of cortex actin showing no significant difference (Figure 4A, B).

claim: FMNL2 depletion caused a significant decrease in cytoplasmic actin signals in mouse oocytes.
source: However, we found a significant decrease of cytoplasmic actin signals in the FMNL2-KD oocytes, and the statistical analysis for the cytoplasmic actin fluorescent signals also confirmed our findings (58.25 ± 2.05, n = 26 vs. 37.92 ± 2.02, n = 24, p < 0.0001, Figure 4C, D).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence intensity analysis showing significantly reduced cytoplasmic actin (Figure 4C, D).

claim: Similar cytoplasmic actin reduction was observed in porcine oocytes after FMNL2 depletion.
source: Similar results were also observed in porcine oocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data from porcine oocytes showing decreased cytoplasmic actin intensity after FMNL2 antibody injection (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: Exogenous FMNL2 rescued the decrease of cytoplasmic actin filaments in FMNL2-depleted oocytes.
source: Moreover, the rescue experiments showed that exogenous FMNL2 rescued the decrease of cytoplasmic actin filaments compared with the FMNL2-depletion group (37.98 ± 1.98, n = 16 vs. 54.72 ± 2.88, n = 15, p < 0.0001, Figure 4E, F).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing restored cytoplasmic actin levels (Figure 4E, F).

claim: FMNL2 precipitated Arp2 and Formin2 but not Profilin and fascin.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation results showed that FMNL2 precipitated Arp2 and Formin2 but not Profilin and fascin (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing protein-protein interactions (Figure 4H).

claim: Arp2 protein expression increased significantly after FMNL2 knockdown.
source: The results showed Arp2 protein expression increased significantly after FMNL2 knockdown (1 vs. 1.56 ± 0.07, p < 0.001, Figure 4I)
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing increased Arp2 protein levels (Figure 4I).

claim: Formin2 protein expression decreased after FMNL2 knockdown.
source: but Formin2 decreased after FMNL2 knockdown (1 vs. 0.62 ± 0.04, p < 0.001, Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing decreased Formin2 protein levels (Figure 4J).

claim: Exogenous FMNL2 rescued the alterations in Arp2 protein expression caused by FMNL2 knockdown.
source: Exogenous FMNL2 rescued these alterations compared with that in the FMNL2-KD group (Arp2 protein expression: 1 vs. 0.65 ± 0.06, p < 0.01, Figure 4I; Formin2 protein expression: 1 vs. 1.24 ± 0.05, p < 0.01, Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing restored Arp2 protein levels (Figure 4I).

claim: Exogenous FMNL2 rescued the alterations in Formin2 protein expression caused by FMNL2 knockdown.
source: Exogenous FMNL2 rescued these alterations compared with that in the FMNL2-KD group (Arp2 protein expression: 1 vs. 0.65 ± 0.06, p < 0.01, Figure 4I; Formin2 protein expression: 1 vs. 1.24 ± 0.05, p < 0.01, Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing restored Formin2 protein levels (Figure 4J).

claim: FMNL2 interacted with INF2 in mouse oocytes.
source: The co-immunoprecipitation results showed that FMNL2 precipitated INF2 and INF2 also precipitated FMNL2 (Figure 5B), indicating that FMNL2 interacted with INF2 in mouse oocytes.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing reciprocal protein interactions (Figure 5B).

claim: In FMNL2-KD oocytes, the ER forms clusters in the cytoplasm in addition to being concentrated around the spindle.
source: As shown in Figure 5C, in control oocytes the ER is highly concentrated around the spindle; however, in the FMNL2-KD oocytes, in addition to being concentrated around the spindle, the ER also forms clusters in the cytoplasm (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging showing altered ER distribution patterns (Figure 5C).

claim: The abnormal distribution of ER increased significantly in the FMNL2-KD group.
source: The statistical analysis showed that the abnormal distribution of ER increased significantly in the FMNL2-KD group (28.91 ± 5.62%, n = 27 vs. 59.64 ± 6.95%, n = 28, p < 0.05, Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of ER distribution patterns (Figure 5D).

claim: Similar ER distribution defects were observed in porcine oocytes after FMNL2 depletion.
source: Similar results were also observed in porcine oocytes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data from porcine oocytes showing increased abnormal ER after FMNL2 antibody injection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: The expressions of ER-stress-related proteins Grp78 and Chop were significantly increased in FMNL2-KD oocytes.
source: In FMNL2-KD oocytes, we found the expressions of ER-stress-related proteins Grp78 and Chop were significantly increased (Grp78: 1 vs. 1.42 ± 0.12, p < 0.05; Chop: 1 vs. 1.53 ± 0.16, p < 0.05, Figure 5E), indicating the occurrence of ER stress.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing increased Grp78 and Chop protein levels (Figure 5E).

claim: Exogenous Fmnl2 mRNA rescued the ER distribution defects caused by FMNL2 knockdown.
source: Supplementing with exogenous Fmnl2 mRNA rescued the ER distribution defects caused by FMNL2 knockdown (Figure 5F), which was supported by the statistical analysis showing that the abnormal distribution rate of ER decreased significantly in the rescue group (52.04 ± 5.29%, n = 70 vs. 34.91 ± 3.37%, n = 78, p < 0.05, Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing restored ER distribution patterns (Figure 5F, 5G).

claim: Grp78 protein expression decreased in the rescue group compared to FMNL2-KD group.
source: Moreover, Grp78 protein expression decreased in the rescue group (1 vs. 0.78 ± 0.05, p < 0.01, Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing reduced Grp78 levels in rescue experiments (Figure 5H).

claim: In FMNL2-KD oocytes, mitochondria form clusters in the cytoplasm in addition to being concentrated around the spindle.
source: In control oocytes, the mitochondria evenly distributed in the cytoplasm and accumulated at the spindle periphery in MI stage; however, in FMNL2-KD oocytes, in addition to being concentrated around the spindle, the mitochondria also forms clusters in the cytoplasm (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging showing altered mitochondrial distribution patterns (Figure 6B).

claim: The uniform distribution of mitochondria decreased significantly in the FMNL2-KD group.
source: We counted the number of clumps in cytoplasm and found that the uniform distribution of mitochondria decreased significantly in the FMNL2-KD group (59.66 ± 8.48%, n = 31 vs. 20.83 ± 4.17%, n = 32, p < 0.05, Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of mitochondrial distribution patterns (Figure 6C).

claim: A large number of FMNL2-KD oocytes showed mitochondria agglomerated into one to three clumps.
source: A large number of FMNL2-KD oocytes agglomerated into one to three clumps (22.73 ± 4.27%, n = 31 vs. 42.50 ± 1.25%, n = 32, p < 0.05, Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of mitochondrial clustering patterns (Figure 6C).

claim: Similar mitochondrial distribution defects were observed in porcine oocytes after FMNL2 depletion.
source: Similar results were also observed in porcine oocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data from porcine oocytes showing increased abnormal mitochondria after FMNL2 antibody injection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: Exogenous Fmnl2 mRNA rescued the mitochondria distribution defects in FMNL2-depleted oocytes.
source: Supplementing with exogenous Fmnl2 mRNA rescued the mitochondria distribution (Figure 6D), the statistical analysis showed that the uniform distribution of mitochondria increased significantly in the rescue group (36.49 ± 3.97%, n = 53 vs. 53.90 ± 2.09%, n = 79, p < 0.05, Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing restored mitochondrial distribution patterns (Figure 6D, 6E).

claim: FMNL2 depletion caused alterations in mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) as measured by JC-1 staining.
source: We also examined mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP), and the results showed that FMNL2 depletion caused the alterations of MMP by JC-1 staining after culturing oocytes in vitro for 9 hr. The fluorescence intensity of JC-1 red channel was decreased compared with the control group (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by JC-1 staining showing decreased red fluorescence intensity (Figure 6F).

claim: The ratio of red/green fluorescence intensity of JC-1 was significantly reduced in FMNL2-KD oocytes.
source: We also calculated the ratio for red/green fluorescence intensity, and the results also confirmed this (control group: 0.40 vs. FMNL2-KD: 0.21 ± 0.01, p < 0.01) (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of JC-1 red/green fluorescence ratios (Figure 6G).

claim: Cofilin protein expression decreased significantly after FMNL2 knockdown.
source: We also examined cofilin protein expression after FMNL2 knockdown. The results showed cofilin protein expression decreased significantly after FMNL2 knockdown (1 vs. 0.81 ± 0.03, p < 0.01, Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing decreased cofilin protein levels (Figure 6H).

claim: Mammalian oocyte maturation is an asymmetric division process that generates a large egg and a small polar body.
source: Mammalian oocyte maturation is an asymmetric division process that generates a large egg and a small polar body.
evidence: This is established knowledge about oocyte maturation.

claim: After germinal vesicle breakdown, the meiotic spindle is organized at the center of the oocyte, and then it migrates to the oocyte cortex at the late metaphase I (MI).
source: After germinal vesicle breakdown, the meiotic spindle is organized at the center of the oocyte, and then it migrates to the oocyte cortex at the late metaphase I (MI). The oocytes are arrested at metaphase II (MII) after the extrusion of first polar body (Pan and Li, 2019; Yi et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Pan and Li, 2019; Yi et al., 2013a).

claim: Actin filaments regulate various dynamic events during oocyte meiotic maturation.
source: Actin filaments, as the most widely distributed cytoskeleton in cells, regulate various dynamic events during oocyte meiotic maturation (Sun and Schatten, 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Sun and Schatten, 2006).

claim: Two key events regulated by actin are the spindle migration and cortical reorganization in mammalian oocytes.
source: and two key events are the spindle migration and cortical reorganization in mammalian oocytes (Duan and Sun, 2019; Sun and Kim, 2013; Yi et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Duan and Sun, 2019; Sun and Kim, 2013; Yi et al., 2013a).

claim: The Arp2/3 complex controls the assembly of branched actin.
source: The actin nucleation factors are the molecules that directly promote the actin assembly: Arp2/3 complex control the assembly of branched actin, and formin family member Formin2 (FMN2) and Spire1/2 control the assembly of linear actin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about actin nucleation factors.

claim: Formin family member Formin2 (FMN2) and Spire1/2 control the assembly of linear actin.
source: The actin nucleation factors are the molecules that directly promote the actin assembly: Arp2/3 complex control the assembly of branched actin, and formin family member Formin2 (FMN2) and Spire1/2 control the assembly of linear actin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about actin nucleation factors.

claim: The cortex protein Arp2/3 complex nucleates the actin to produce a hydrodynamic force to move the spindle toward the cortex.
source: The cortex protein Arp2/3 complex nucleates the actin to produce a hydrodynamic force to move the spindle toward the cortex, and regulates cytokinesis during oocyte maturation (Sun et al., 2011; Yi et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Sun et al., 2011; Yi et al., 2013a).

claim: FMN2 and Spire1/2 nucleate actin around the spindle in the cytoplasm to give the meiotic spindle an initial power for migration.
source: FMN2 and Spire1/2 nucleates actin around the spindle in the cytoplasm to give the meiotic spindle an initial power for migration (Li et al., 2008; Pfender et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Li et al., 2008; Pfender et al., 2011).

claim: The DRFs family consists of mDia, Daam, FHOD, and FMNLs.
source: The DRFs family consists of mDia, Daam, FHOD, and FMNLs (Kühn and Geyer, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Kühn and Geyer, 2014).

claim: The 'Formin-like' proteins (FMNLs) subfamily includes FMNL1 (FRL1), FMNL2 (FRL3), and FMNL3 (FRL2).
source: The 'Formin-like' proteins (FMNLs) subfamily includes FMNL1 (FRL1), FMNL2 (FRL3), and FMNL3 (FRL2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the FMNL subfamily.

claim: FMNLs play important roles in cell migration, cell division, and cell polarity.
source: Like other Formin family proteins, FMNLs play important roles in cell migration, cell division, and cell polarity (Katoh and Katoh, 2003; Kühn and Geyer, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Katoh and Katoh, 2003; Kühn and Geyer, 2014).

claim: FMNL2 is widely expressed in multiple human tissues, especially in the gastrointestinal and mammary epithelia, lymphatic tissues, placenta, and reproductive tract.
source: While FMNL2 is widely expressed in multiple human tissues, especially in the gastrointestinal and mammary epithelia, lymphatic tissues, placenta, and reproductive tract (Gardberg et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Gardberg et al., 2010).

claim: FMNL2 accelerates the elongation of actin filaments branched by Arp2/3 complex.
source: As an important actin assembly factor, FMNL2 accelerates the elongation of actin filaments branched by Arp2/3 complex (Kage et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Kage et al., 2017).

claim: In invasive cells, FMNL2 is mainly localized in the leading edge of the cell, lamellipodia and filopodia tips.
source: In invasive cells, FMNL2 is mainly localized in the leading edge of the cell, lamellipodia and filopodia tips, to improve cell migration ability by actin-based manner (Block et al., 2012; Kage et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Block et al., 2012; Kage et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2011).

claim: FMNL2 is involved in the maintenance of epithelial–mesenchymal transition in human colorectal carcinoma cell.
source: FMNL2 is also involved in the maintenance of epithelial–mesenchymal transition in human colorectal carcinoma cell (Li et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Li et al., 2010).

claim: The absence of FMNL2/3 can cause Golgi fragmentation.
source: It is shown that FMNL2 is related with the Golgi apparatus, since the absence of FMNL2/3 can cause the Golgi fragmentation (Kage et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Kage et al., 2019).

claim: FMNL2 might interact with organelle dynamics.
source: Besides its roles on the actin assembly, emerging evidences indicate that FMNL2 may interact with organelle dynamics.
evidence: Based on inference from emerging evidence mentioned in the text.

claim: The roles of FMNLs especially FMNL2 on oocyte meiosis are still largely unknown.
source: However, till now the roles of FMNLs especially FMNL2 on oocyte meiosis are still largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: FMNL2 is essential for the polar body size control and successful extrusion.
source: Our results showed that FMNL2 was essential for the polar body size control and successful extrusion
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing polar body extrusion defects and large polar bodies after FMNL2 depletion.

claim: The abnormal phenotypes caused by FMNL2 depletion might be due to aberrant actin-based meiotic spindle migration.
source: and these abnormal phenotypes might be due to aberrant actin-based meiotic spindle migration.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations of spindle migration defects and actin changes.

claim: FMNL2 was essential for the functions and distribution of mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: Meanwhile, we also found that FMNL2 was essential for the functions and distribution of mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing altered ER and mitochondrial distribution and function after FMNL2 depletion.

claim: FMNL2 associates with Formin2 and Arp2/3 complex for actin assembly.
source: Therefore, this study provided the evidence for the critical roles of FMNL2-mediated actin on spindle movement and organelle dynamics in mammalian oocytes.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data and protein expression changes.

claim: FMNL2-mediated actin regulates spindle migration and INF2/Cofilin-related organelle dynamics during mouse and porcine oocyte maturation.
source: Collectively, we provide a body of evidence showing that FMNL2 associates with Formin2 and Arp2/3 complex for actin assembly, which further regulates spindle migration and INF2/Cofilin-related organelle dynamics during mammalian oocyte maturation.
evidence: Supported by comprehensive experimental data from multiple assays showing FMNL2's roles in actin assembly, spindle migration, and organelle dynamics.

claim: The asymmetry defects of oocytes will lead to the failure of fertilization and embryo implantation.
source: The asymmetry defects of oocytes will lead to the failure of fertilization and embryo implantation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the consequences of oocyte asymmetry defects.

claim: This asymmetry is critical for the following fertilization and early embryo development.
source: This asymmetry is critical for the following fertilization and early embryo development.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the importance of oocyte asymmetry.

claim: FMNL2 might be involved in cytokinesis and asymmetric division by regulating actin assembly during mouse oocyte maturation.
source: These results suggested that FMNL2 might be involved in cytokinesis and asymmetric division by regulating actin assembly during mouse oocyte maturation.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations of polar body defects and cytoplasmic actin changes.

claim: The spindle migration is a key step in ensuring the asymmetric division for oocytes.
source: The spindle migration is a key step in ensuring the asymmetric division for oocytes (Brunet and Maro, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Brunet and Maro, 2005).

claim: In mitosis, spindle position is decided by cortical actin and astral microtubules.
source: In mitosis, spindle position is decided by cortical actin and astral microtubules; in contrast, spindle migration is mainly mediated by actin filaments during oocyte meiosis (Brunet and Maro, 2005; Reinsch and Gönczy, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Brunet and Maro, 2005; Reinsch and Gönczy, 1998).

claim: Spindle migration is mainly mediated by actin filaments during oocyte meiosis.
source: In mitosis, spindle position is decided by cortical actin and astral microtubules; in contrast, spindle migration is mainly mediated by actin filaments during oocyte meiosis (Brunet and Maro, 2005; Reinsch and Gönczy, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Brunet and Maro, 2005; Reinsch and Gönczy, 1998).

claim: FMN2 nucleates actin surrounding the spindle, with pushing force generated by actin triggering spindle migration.
source: For example, FMN2 nucleates actin surrounding the spindle, pushing force generated by actin to trigger the spindle migration (Duan et al., 2020; Dumont et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Duan et al., 2020; Dumont et al., 2007).

claim: Cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (Cdk1) induces cytoplasmic Formin-mediated F-actin polymerization to propel the spindle into the cortex.
source: and cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (Cdk1) induces cytoplasmic Formin-mediated F-actin polymerization to propel the spindle into the cortex (Wei et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Wei et al., 2018).

claim: Absence of the formin family member FMNL1 or FHOD1 could lead to the decrease of cytoplasmic actin to prevent the spindle migration.
source: Our previous studies also showed that absence of the formin family member FMNL1 or FHOD1 could lead to the decrease of cytoplasmic actin to prevent the spindle migration (Pan et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Pan et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015).

claim: FMNL2 together with other Formin proteins conservatively regulate actin-mediated spindle migration during oocyte meiosis.
source: We speculated that FMNL2 together with other Formin proteins, conservatively regulate actin-mediated spindle migration during oocyte meiosis.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and comparison with other formin proteins.

claim: Proper distribution of ER is important for the oocyte quality.
source: Proper distribution of ER is important for the oocyte quality.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ER function in oocytes.

claim: ER displays a homogeneous distribution pattern throughout the entire ooplasm during development of oocytes and embryos from diabetic mice.
source: ER displays a homogeneous distribution pattern throughout the entire ooplasm during development of oocytes and embryos from diabetic mice (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Zhang et al., 2013).

claim: During the transition of mouse oocytes from MI to MII phase, actin regulates cortical ER aggregation.
source: During the transition of mouse oocytes from MI to MII phase, actin regulates cortical ER aggregation (FitzHarris et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (FitzHarris et al., 2007).

claim: Formin2 colocalizes with the ER during oocyte meiosis.
source: In addition, Formin2 is shown to colocalize with the ER during oocyte meiosis and the ER-associated Formin2 at the spindle periphery is required for MI chromosome migration (Yi et al., 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Yi et al., 2013b).

claim: The ER-associated Formin2 at the spindle periphery is required for MI chromosome migration.
source: In addition, Formin2 is shown to colocalize with the ER during oocyte meiosis and the ER-associated Formin2 at the spindle periphery is required for MI chromosome migration (Yi et al., 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Yi et al., 2013b).

claim: INF2 is an ER-associated protein.
source: In our results, we showed that FMNL2 associated with INF2 protein in oocytes. INF2 is an ER-associated protein
evidence: This is established knowledge about INF2.

claim: The expression of GFP-INF2 containing DAD/WH2 mutations causes the ER to collapse around the nucleus.
source: and the expression of GFP-INF2 which containing DAD/WH2 mutations causes the ER to collapse around the nucleus (Chhabra et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Chhabra et al., 2009).

claim: FMNL2 might regulate INF2 for the distribution of ER in cytoplasm of oocytes.
source: We concluded that FMNL2 might regulate INF2 for the distribution of ER in cytoplasm of oocytes.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing FMNL2-INF2 interaction and ER distribution defects.

claim: INF2 affects mitochondrial length and ER–mitochondrial interaction in an actin-dependent manner.
source: Besides its roles of ER distribution, it is shown that INF2 also affects mitochondrial length and ER–mitochondrial interaction in an actin-dependent manner (Chhabra et al., 2009; Korobova et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Chhabra et al., 2009; Korobova et al., 2013).

claim: INF2 regulates Drp1 for mitochondrial fission.
source: It is shown that INF2 regulates Drp1 for mitochondrial fission, and INF2-induced actin filaments may drive initial mitochondrial constriction, which allows Drp1-driven secondary constriction (Ji et al., 2017; Korobova et al., 2013).
